title: Leased but Undrilled
metaTitle: Selling Leased but Undrilled Mineral Rights in West Virginia
metaDescription: Signed a West Virginia lease, banked the bonus, and no rig has shown up? We buy leased, undrilled mineral rights and factor the lease terms into the price.
heroLead: A signed lease with no well on it is a bet the operator hasn't decided to make yet, and that uncertainty is exactly what we price when we look at an undrilled tract.
intro: Plenty of West Virginia mineral owners signed a lease during the 2008-2014 land rush, cashed a bonus check, and then watched years go by with no drilling activity on their tract at all. Some of those leases have since expired and were never renewed. Others are still held, either by a producing well elsewhere in the unit, by a shut-in clause, or by continuous delay rental payments the operator keeps current without ever committing to drill.

We buy leased, undrilled interests regularly. The lease terms themselves, primary term length, whether it's held by production from a neighboring well, and what royalty rate it specifies, all factor directly into what we can offer.

sections.heading: Reading what your lease actually says now
paragraphs: The first thing we check is whether the lease is still in effect. Most West Virginia leases from this era carried a primary term of three to five years, extendable if the operator is paying delay rentals or if the tract has been pooled into a unit with a producing well elsewhere, even if no well sits on your specific acreage. If none of those conditions apply and the primary term has run out, the lease may have lapsed entirely, which changes your interest from a leased asset to an unleased one, generally a different, often higher, value proposition.
We pull the recorded lease and any amendments or unit designation orders filed against it to determine exactly where it stands before quoting a number.

sections.heading: Why held-by-production status matters more than most owners realize
paragraphs: If your tract was pooled into a unit and a well elsewhere in that unit is producing, your lease is likely held indefinitely even though no well sits on your specific acreage and you're not currently receiving a royalty check. That's a meaningfully different situation from a lease that's simply sitting on delay rentals waiting for a drilling decision, because held-by-production status means the operator has already committed capital to the general area and the lease isn't going anywhere on its own.

We check the unit designation records at the county clerk's office to confirm whether your tract is inside an established unit versus outside one, since that materially affects how we think about timing and value.

sections.heading: What happens if the lease expires before any well is drilled
paragraphs: If your primary term runs out with no drilling, no pooling into a unit, and no delay rentals being paid, the lease has likely lapsed and the mineral rights revert to being unleased. Some owners in that position want to wait and see if a new operator leases the tract again, which can take an unpredictable amount of time depending on activity in your county. Others would rather sell the interest outright now rather than wait through another uncertain leasing cycle.
We're comfortable buying either leased-and-held or fully unleased tracts, and we'll tell you plainly which category your interest falls into once we've reviewed the recorded documents.

sections.heading: What we look at before making an offer
paragraphs: We want the lease itself, any amendments or ratifications, and if the tract has been pooled, the unit designation order recorded with the state. From those documents we can tell whether you're sitting on a held tract with real near-term development potential or a lease that's effectively dormant, and price the interest accordingly rather than guessing off the original bonus amount.

faqs.question: My lease's primary term already ended. Am I still under contract?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. If there's no producing well in a pooled unit covering your tract and no delay rentals being paid, the lease may have lapsed. We check the recorded lease and any unit filings to confirm the current status.

faqs.question: Why hasn't a well been drilled on my tract yet?
faqs.answer: Operators often lease broadly and then drill only the acreage that fits their current development plan, which can leave individual tracts undrilled for years even inside an active area. It reflects the operator's pace and pad location choices, not necessarily a problem with your title.

faqs.question: Is my leased, undrilled interest worth less than a producing one?
faqs.answer: Typically yes, since there's no current royalty income and drilling timing is uncertain. But it still has real value, particularly if it's held by production in a pooled unit, and we price that uncertainty explicitly rather than ignoring it.

faqs.question: Can I sell if my lease has already expired?
faqs.answer: Yes. An expired lease generally means your rights are unleased, which is a different, often more straightforward, situation to value and sell than an interest still tied up in an active lease.

faqs.question: What is a shut-in royalty clause and does mine have one?
faqs.answer: A shut-in clause lets an operator hold a lease with a small annual payment when a well capable of production isn't currently producing, often for market or pipeline reasons. We check your lease's specific language, since not all West Virginia leases from this era include one.
